title: How to Check an Off-Plan Developer's Promises Before You Buy
seoTitle: How to Check an Off-Plan Developer's Promises
description: A free check any off-plan buyer can do in ten minutes: compare a developer's old launch renderings with what Google Street View shows today.
answer: Find a project the same developer launched five to ten years ago, look up its original renderings or fly-through video, then open the same address in Google Street View. The gap between what was promised and what was built tells you how far to trust the new project.
body:
Every developer tells the same story at launch: this is the deal of your life. That story is part of the job. Your job as a buyer is different. You need to decide how much of it to believe, and there is a simple way to do that before you sign anything.

## The Street View test

1. **Find an older project by the same developer.** Search for their launches from five to ten years ago, for example a project announced in 2015 or 2017 that should be finished by now.
2. **Find the launch material.** Renderings and fly-through videos often stay online for years, on the developer's site, on broker pages or on YouTube.
3. **Open the same address in Google Maps and Street View.** Look at the building that actually exists today.
4. **Compare.** Facade, materials, landscaping, the street around it, the height. Was the vision delivered, upgraded, or quietly cut back?

The gap between the first image and the last one is the most honest review a developer will ever get.

## Buy the data, not the narrative

A launch is built to sell a feeling. Renderings are taken from the best angle, in the best light, usually of the best unit. That is marketing, and it is fine. But your decision should rest on data: the history of the developer, the layout of your exact unit, the real view from your windows, the finishes you will actually get.

## When the data is missing

If you ask for specific information and receive more lifestyle images instead, treat that as a red flag. A developer with a strong record and a solid project has every reason to show you precise details. A developer who gives you a lot of dream and very little data is telling you something too.

Doing this check takes ten minutes. Skipping it can cost you years of waiting for a building that never looks like the brochure.
takeaways: A developer's past projects are the best predictor of the next one.
Compare old launch renderings with today's Street View of the same address.
Base your decision on data about your unit, not on the launch story.
Lots of lifestyle images and little hard information is a red flag.
faq: How do I find a developer's old renderings?

Search the developer's name with the project name and the launch year, and look on their website archive, broker listings and YouTube. Fly-through videos and launch brochures often stay online for years.
What if the developer has no finished projects?
Then you are taking a larger risk. Look at the track record of the general contractor, the architect and the people behind the company, and expect the price to reflect that extra risk.
Is a small difference between rendering and reality a problem?
Not necessarily. Some changes are normal during construction. What matters is the pattern: a developer who consistently delivers less than promised will likely do it again.
